Teo had been in the Riverside Youth Orchestra for three weeks when Mr. Haddad handed him the cymbal part for the last movement of the symphony. It was a single page. Most of it was a long line of rests, numbered in small print above the staff, and near the bottom, after two hundred and twelve bars of silence, there was one note: a crash, marked fortissimo, with an accent over it.

"That's it?" Teo asked.

"That's it," said Mrs. Lund, who played timpani and had sat in the orchestra's back row for longer than most of its members had been alive. "Don't miss it."

At home he made a chart. He wrote the numbers one to two hundred and twelve on a sheet of graph paper and practiced counting along with a recording, tapping each bar on his knee and crossing off the numbers in pencil. By Thursday he could reach the crash and land it within a breath of the recording.

At Saturday's rehearsal he came in early. Mr. Haddad slowed the tempo in the middle of the movement, as the recording never did, and Teo, counting at the speed he had practiced, brought the cymbals together in the middle of a quiet passage for flute. The sound filled the hall. Two violinists turned around.

Afterward Mrs. Lund found him packing the cymbals into their case. She asked to see his chart, looked at it for a while, and handed it back.

"Counting is fine for the first hundred," she said. "After that, listen for the horns. They have a tune just before you, eight notes going up, and on the last one you come in. The horns will be there whatever speed he takes."

Teo said he had never noticed the horns.

"Of course," she said. "You were busy with your arithmetic."

For the next week he listened to the recording without the chart. The first time through, the horn tune went by before he recognized it. The second time he caught it halfway. By the fifth he could hum it, and once he knew it he could hear it coming several bars away, the way you hear your own name across a noisy room.

On the night of the concert Mr. Haddad took the last movement faster than the recording, faster than he had ever taken it in rehearsal. Teo sat with his hands through the cymbal straps and his eyes on the horn section. He had lost count somewhere around ninety and let it go. When the horns raised their instruments and began to climb, he rose, and on the eighth note he brought the cymbals together.

Mrs. Lund, behind the timpani, gave a single nod without looking up.

At the reception his mother asked whether it had been dull to sit through all that music for one note. Teo said it was the opposite. He had spent the whole movement following the horns, and before the horns the cellos, whose line led into theirs. It had been, he told her, the busiest he had ever been while sitting still.

Every evening, at the hour the porch light comes on,
she begins again: the brown spider
no bigger than my thumbnail
who lives where the gutter meets the post.

First a single thread, let out on the wind
until it snags on the railing six feet away,
and she walks it, testing, the way a person
crosses a creek on a fallen log.

Then the spokes, dropped one by one
from that first line, a wheel
that has only its spokes,
and then the spiral, around and around,

her back legs measuring each gap
before she fixes the next turn in place,
so the rings lie as evenly spaced
as the lines on a sheet of notebook paper.

It takes her about an hour.
I have timed her by the kitchen clock.
When the moths come to the light
she is hanging head-down at the center.

By morning the web is torn,
a hole where something heavy went through,
the threads beaded with dew and sagging.
She takes it down herself. She eats it,

I read later in a field guide,
rolling the old silk into a ball
and swallowing her own work
so she can spin it out again at dusk.

All summer I have watched her do this:
build the whole thing, lose it, eat it, build.
My father says she must be tired of it,
the same web every night for nothing.

I think he is watching the wrong part.
Each night the first thread lands somewhere new,
the railing, the mailbox, once the handlebar of my bike,
and she has to work out the rest from there,

a different web on a different frame,
every angle figured fresh,
and by the time the moths come, she has.

The summer I was thirteen, my brother Sam and I took the train across three states to spend a month with our aunt in Halford. Sam was nineteen and in charge of the tickets. I was his little brother and in charge of everything else, or believed I was. I had the railroad's printed timetable, and I had gone through it with a red pen, circling each stop where there was something to see and writing beside it what we would see: a river crossing at dawn, a tunnel through the Corder Hills, a bridge so long the timetable gave it a line of its own.

For the first day the train kept to my schedule almost to the minute. I checked each station against my watch and drew a line through it as we left. Sam slept, or read, or bought us sandwiches from the dining car, and every hour or so he asked me where we were, which I suspect now was a kindness.

On the second morning the train slowed in the middle of a wheat field and stopped at a town called Ardel. A conductor came through to explain that a freight train had come off the rails forty miles ahead. We would be here, he said, until the track was cleared, probably for the rest of the day.

I found Ardel in the timetable. It had no red circle. The line beside it read only "4:12 a.m., 2 min." On schedule, we would have slept straight through it.

Sam put his book away and said we might as well see the place. In my second year of high school I owned a yellow highlighter that ran dry about every three weeks. I used it on everything. Before a chemistry test I would open the textbook to the chapter, read it slowly, and drag the marker across every sentence that seemed important, which by the end of an evening was most of them. Then I would read the yellow parts again. The pages glowed. I felt ready, and I usually got a C.

My friend Ana studied differently, and at first her method looked to me like a waste of time. She would read the chapter once, close the book, and write on index cards every question she could think of. Then she would try to answer them from memory, moving a card to a separate pile each time she missed it. It was slow and uncomfortable to watch. Half the time she sat staring at a card, getting nowhere.

Ana got A's. When I finally asked why she did it the hard way, she said that rereading told her what was on the page, but the cards told her what was in her head, and the two were different.

She was right, and researchers who study memory have reported much the same thing for decades. In experiments, students who spend part of their study time trying to recall material with the book closed generally remember more of it a week later than students who spend the same time reading it again. The effect has turned up with word lists, science passages, and history facts, and among learners of many ages.

Part of the reason seems to be that reading a page a second time feels easy. The words are familiar, and familiarity is easily mistaken for knowledge. I recognized every sentence I had highlighted, so I assumed I knew it. But recognizing an answer in front of you is a different skill from producing it once the page is gone, and a test asks for the second.

The struggle that made Ana's method look so poor turns out to be part of why it works. Each miss showed her exactly where the gaps were, and the effort of pulling an answer out of memory seems to make that answer easier to find the next time.

I have nothing against highlighters. A stripe of yellow can help a reader find a passage again. But I have come to distrust the comfortable feeling of moving my eyes across a page I already know. These days, when studying feels easy, I take it as a sign to close the book.

The Harn watered every farm in the lower valley, and on the territory's maps it was a confident blue line that simply stopped where the surveyed country ended. Cut a large hailstone in half and you will often find that it is built like an onion, in layers. Some rings are clear as window glass; others are milky white. For a long time these rings were explained by a simple story, and that story has turned out to be only partly right.

Hail forms inside thunderstorms, in clouds that can tower many miles into the sky. Even in summer the upper parts of such a cloud are well below freezing, and they hold vast numbers of supercooled droplets: tiny drops of water that stay liquid below the freezing point because they have nothing to freeze onto.

A hailstone begins as a small particle of ice, often a soft pellet or a frozen raindrop, called the embryo. As it moves through the cloud, supercooled droplets strike it and freeze to its surface, and it grows. What keeps it aloft while it grows is the storm's updraft, a column of rising air that in strong storms can hold up a stone the size of a golf ball or larger. When the stone grows too heavy for the updraft to support, or drifts out of it, the stone falls.

The look of each layer records the conditions in which it formed. Where the air is very cold and the droplets are few, each droplet freezes almost the instant it hits, trapping tiny bubbles of air, and the ice comes out cloudy. Where droplets are plentiful and the temperature is closer to freezing, the water has time to spread over the stone before it freezes, the air escapes, and the ice is clear.

The old story held that a hailstone gets its layers by riding the updraft up and falling back again and again, adding a ring on each trip, so that a stone with five rings had made five loops through the cloud. Recent studies, some using computer models of storms and some analyzing the water frozen into individual layers, suggest that many hailstones make only one or two such trips. A stone can collect several layers during a single passage simply by moving through regions of different temperature and moisture along the way.

So the rings are less like the rings of a tree, one for each year, and more like the entries in a travel diary: a record of where the stone went, written as it passed. That makes a hailstone a remarkable kind of messenger. It carries an account of the inside of a storm, a place where few instruments can safely go, and delivers it to the ground for anyone willing to cut it open and read it.

Cut a large hailstone in half and you will often find that it is built like an onion, in layers. Some rings are clear as window glass; others are milky white. For a long time these rings were explained by a simple story, and that story has turned out to be only partly right.

Hail forms inside thunderstorms, in clouds that can tower many miles into the sky. Even in summer the upper parts of such a cloud are well below freezing, and they hold vast numbers of supercooled droplets: tiny drops of water that stay liquid below the freezing point because they have nothing to freeze onto.

A hailstone begins as a small particle of ice, often a soft pellet or a frozen raindrop, called the embryo. As it moves through the cloud, supercooled droplets strike it and freeze to its surface, and it grows. What keeps it aloft while it grows is the storm's updraft, a column of rising air that in strong storms can hold up a stone the size of a golf ball or larger. When the stone grows too heavy for the updraft to support, or drifts out of it, the stone falls.

The look of each layer records the conditions in which it formed. Where the air is very cold and the droplets are few, each droplet freezes almost the instant it hits, trapping tiny bubbles of air, and the ice comes out cloudy. Where droplets are plentiful and the temperature is closer to freezing, the water has time to spread over the stone before it freezes, the air escapes, and the ice is clear.
